rationale: A wins because it found the sharpest real risk in the update and made it pitch-shaped: "Anker says its home battery needs no major rewiring. Installers will decide if that's true." B has competent bones, but it leaves that story half-buried as proof under "Anker takes on Tesla Powerwall with a US home battery launch." A also tells the founder when not to pitch; B too often says pick a shape and proceed, which is how you walk a founder into a reporter's buzz saw.
gaps_in_A: "Powerwall has defined" imports a market framing not supplied in the update. It is plausible, but a blind judge should not have to grant it for free.

"A profitable charger maker bets on a capital-heavy market" is the thinnest angle, and A admits it: "Right now the facts support only 'large, profitable, publicly traded,' which is a description, not a story." Good self-policing, but still a weak inclusion.

"The prevailing belief is that whole-home batteries mean panel work, transfer switches, and an electrician's week" is useful trade context, but it is not in the supplied facts and needs sourcing before it becomes pitch language.
gaps_in_B: "Anker naming Tesla Powerwall as direct competition" overstates the given fact. The update says Anker competes with Tesla Powerwall; it does not say Anker named Tesla or explicitly positioned against it.
"Tesla publishes warranty terms on Powerwall" is an outside claim not supplied in the update. It may be true, but in this exercise it is still an invented support beam.

"Story type: category-creation" is the wrong label. Home battery storage already exists in the facts because Anker competes with Tesla Powerwall and others; this is entry/diversification, not category creation.

B misses the best contrarian angle as a standalone story. The "without major electrical rewiring" claim belongs with installers, permits, panels, and verification, not as a side question inside the Tesla comparison.
